en: Majjhima Nikāya 59,
Bahuvedanīyasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga approached the Venerable Udāyī;
having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Udāyī and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable Udāyī, how many kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One?
“Carpenter, three kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
“These, carpenter, are the three feelings spoken of by the Blessed One.
When this was said, the carpenter Pañcakanga said to the Venerable Udāyin:
“Venerable Udāyin, it is not the case that three feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One;”
“Two kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One—
the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling.
As for this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, venerable sir, it has been spoken of by the Blessed One as peaceful and sublime happiness.”
A second time, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga:
"Householder, two feelings were not taught by the Blessed One;
three feelings were taught by the Blessed One."
"Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these, head carpenter, are the three feelings spoken of by the Blessed One.
A second time, the head carpenter Pañcakanga said this to the Venerable Udāyin:
“Venerable Udāyin, it is not three feelings that were spoken of by the Blessed One;
two feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One—
the pleasant feeling and the painful feeling.”
“Venerable sir, this feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant has been called by the Blessed One ‘peaceful’ and ‘sublime pleasure.
For a third time, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga:
“Carpenter, two kinds of feeling have not been taught by the Blessed One.”
“Three kinds of feeling have been spoken of by the Blessed One:
pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
These, householder, are the three kinds of feeling spoken of by the Blessed One.”
A third time, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said this to the Venerable Udāyin:
"Venerable Udāyin, three feelings were not spoken of by the Blessed One;
two feelings were spoken of by the Blessed One—namely, pleasant feeling and painful feeling."
“There is pleasant feeling and painful feeling.
But that which, venerable sir, is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—this, bhante, has been called by the Blessed One a peaceful and sublime pleasure.
Yet the Venerable Udāyī was unable to convince the carpenter Pañcakanga, nor was the carpenter Pañcakanga able to convince the Venerable Udāyī.
The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga the carpenter.
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entirety of the conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Udāyī and Pañcakaṅga the carpenter.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, it was indeed a valid method that the carpenter Pañcakaṅga did not approve of for Udāyī, and it was indeed a valid method that Udāyī did not approve of for the carpenter Pañcakaṅga.
For, Ānanda, two feelings have been taught by me according to one method, and three feelings have also been taught by me according to another method, and five as well.”
Feeling has been taught by me through a method; six kinds of feeling have been taught by me through a method; eighteen kinds of feeling have been taught by me through a method;
thirty-six kinds of feeling have been taught by me through a method; one hundred and eight kinds of feeling have been taught by me through a method.
"Thus, Ānanda, has the Dhamma been taught by me through various methods. When the Dhamma has been thus taught by me through various methods,
it is to be expected of those who do not acknowledge, approve of, or rejoice in what has been well-spoken and well-uttered by one another that they will fall into quarrels."
"Having fallen into quarreling and disputes, they will dwell piercing one another with the weapons of the mouth.
Thus, Ānanda, has the Dhamma been taught by me through various methods.
And when the Dhamma has been thus taught by me through various methods, those who [speak] what is well-spoken and well-uttered to one another..."
Those who will assent to it, approve of it, and rejoice in it—for them this is to be expected:
they will dwell in harmony, in mutual affection, without dispute, like milk and water mixed, looking upon one another with eyes of love.
Now, Ānanda, there are these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, dear, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear... [and so on].
Odors cognizable by the nose...
tastes cognizable by the tongue...
tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust—
"These, Ānanda, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
Whatever happiness and gladness arise in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure, this is called sensual pleasure.
If anyone were to say, ‘This is the supreme happiness and gladness that beings experience,’ I do not concede that to him."
And why is that? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness?

“Here, Ānanda, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna … This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
As to anyone who would say: ‘This is the ultimate pleasure and joy that beings experience,’ I do not grant them this.”
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness?
“Here, Ānanda, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that previous happiness.
If anyone, Ānanda, were to say thus...”
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?

Here, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna of which the noble ones declare: "He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily. ... [pe] ...
"Ānanda, this other happiness is indeed more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.
Ānanda, whoever should say... [and so forth].
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as above] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, Ānanda, is that other happiness which is more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
“Ānanda, whoever should say this … [as before] … And what, Ānanda,
is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?”

"Here, Ānanda, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
Whoever, Ānanda, should say..."
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
"Ānanda, this other happiness is indeed more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.
Should anyone, Ānanda, speak thus... [and so on].
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This, Ānanda, is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness.
"Ānanda, whoever should say this... [as before] ...And what, Ānanda,
is that other happiness more excellent and sublime than this happiness?"
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than the former happiness.
As for anyone who would say: ‘Beings experience this as the highest pleasure and joy,’ I do not grant him that.”
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness superior and more sublime than this happiness.
And what, Ānanda, is that other happiness superior and more sublime than this happiness?
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling.
This, Ānanda, is a happiness more excellent and sublime than that other happiness.
It is possible, Ānanda, that wanderers of other sects might say this:"
“The ascetic Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he describes that as happiness.
What is this? How is this? Ānanda, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be told:
“Friend, it is not with reference to pleasant feeling alone that the Blessed One describes [it] as pleasure;
rather, friend, wherever and in whatever way pleasure is found, there and in that way the Tathāgata describes it as pleasure.
This is what the Blessed One said.
The Venerable Ānanda, elated, rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The ninth discourse, the Bahuvedanīyasutta, is concluded.
